subject: Climate & Environment
title: The Keeling Curve
description: A quick win: understand The Keeling Curve.

hook.text: In 1958, Charles Keeling began measuring CO₂ on a Hawaiian volcano. Nobody cared.

buildup.text: His instruments showed CO₂ rising and falling with the seasons, like Earth breathing.

discovery.text: But the baseline kept climbing — year after year, the average never came back down.

twist.text: Keeling's curve became the single most important graph in climate science.

climax.text: CO₂ was 315 ppm when he started. It is over 420 ppm today and still climbing.

punchline.text: One line on a graph told the story of our atmosphere.

quiz.question: What did the Keeling Curve first measure?

details.summary: The Keeling Curve is the continuous measurement of atmospheric CO2 at Mauna Loa, Hawaii, begun by Charles David Keeling in 1958. It shows an unmistakable upward trend from 315 to over 420 ppm with an annual sawtooth pattern reflecting seasonal vegetation cycles.
details.whyItMatters: The Keeling Curve is the single most important dataset in climate science. Its unbroken record made rising CO2 undeniable and anchored decades of policy debate.
takeaways: Measurements began at 315 ppm in 1958 and now exceed 420 ppm
The annual zigzag reflects Northern Hemisphere plant photosynthesis
The record has never shown a year-over-year decline

faq.question: Why was Mauna Loa chosen for CO2 measurements?
faq.answer: Mauna Loa's high altitude, remote Pacific location, and distance from forests and cities ensure that air samples represent well-mixed global atmospheric concentrations rather than local influences from vegetation or industry.

faq.question: What causes the annual zigzag in the Keeling Curve?
faq.answer: Northern Hemisphere forests and crops absorb CO2 during spring and summer growth, pulling concentrations down. In fall and winter, decomposition and reduced photosynthesis release CO2 back, pushing concentrations up. The cycle repeats each year.
